Yesterday we learned that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed, alleging that Apple Photos' facial recognition feature violates state privacy laws.

This case has been conflated with Meta's use of facial recognition, even though the two companies sit at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum. The court's decision to allow the case to proceed shows a fundamental misunderstanding of how the feature works...

The Earlier Lawsuit Against Meta

To properly understand the current situation, we need to look back at a facial recognition lawsuit against Meta, which was filed as early as 2015.

Because that facial recognition was performed on Meta's servers, Meta was able to identify those faces, so the company did indeed break the law and was ultimately ordered to pay $650 million to settle the allegations.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which requires companies to obtain consent before collecting biometric information.

Apple's Approach Is Fundamentally Different

There is a fundamental problem with this allegation: when Apple performs facial recognition within the Apple Photos app, it does not collect any biometric data whatsoever. As Apple described in a machine learning research paper published in 2021, the entire recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

What's more, all the iPhone does is point out that "these photos all appear to be of the same person" — it has absolutely no idea who that person is. The only person who can put a name to that face is the iPhone user themselves.

Apple's privacy policy regarding photos confirms this.

Incredibly, this lawsuit has been grinding its way through the justice system for six years now, and just a few minutes of research would demonstrate that its allegations simply do not hold up.

Courts and legislators should be actively applauding Apple for this kind of privacy-protective approach, rather than conflating it with the privacy-violating practices of companies like Meta.

This is just another example of courts and legislators fundamentally not understanding the technology they are attempting to regulate. The most obvious example, of course, concerns end-to-end encryption — multiple countries have threatened or even attempted to ban end-to-end encryption, despite having no understanding of how it actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every field they are required to touch upon. But they have access to experts, and what I find difficult to comprehend is how these lawsuits and legislative efforts can advance through the system for years with such fundamental errors going unchallenged.
